title: The Hollow Cliffs

pages.text:
*The Fifteenth Rule of Mapmaking: Look up from the paper.*

The sun rose over the Hollow Cliffs, hanging in the sky like a raw egg dropped onto white porcelain. Below, the sea was a churning grey mess, throwing itself against jagged rocks that jutted out into the water like broken teeth. Gulls screamed, a sharp, angry sound that scraped against the silence. The path leading down to the water was no path at all; it was a ledge, a sliver of stone perhaps two feet wide, balanced precariously on the edge of the drop.

Tam stood at the start of it, her knuckles white on the surveying chain. To map this coast honestly, she had to see the full curve from the edge. She had to walk it.

Odd stood beside her, very pale. His red hair looked like it was trying to escape his head. He stared down at the water, then back up at the sky, then down again, his hands shaking violently.

"I can do it," Tam said. Her voice sounded thin in the wind.

"Can you?" Odd asked. He swallowed hard, his throat moving visibly. He looked green, truly green, the color of sea-glass in a tide pool.
pages.image: A narrow stone ledge on a high cliff edge, with a young girl in a patched brown coat holding a chain and a tall boy with red hair looking pale and frightened; jagged white sea stacks and crashing grey waves below; dramatic, high vantage point.

pages.text:
Tam went first. She dropped to her belly, the rock cold and damp against her cheek, while the chain trailed behind her in the grass. It was hard work, and her arms began to burn. The wind tugged at her braid, and the blue string brushed her neck.

She could see, but not far. The curve of the coast bent away from her, hidden by the height of the cliff. If she drew it from here, the line would be wrong. It would be a guess. And a guess is just a lie wearing a nice hat.

She scrambled back up, her knees knocking together. She turned to Odd. He was still standing there, rooted to the spot, his eyes fixed on a single point on the rock face.

"I need a second set of eyes," Tam said. She didn't ask, and she didn't beg. She just stated it, like the weather.

Odd looked at her, then at the ledge, and finally at his own hands, which were still trembling slightly. He nodded.

Tam pulled her knotted rope from her satchel. It was thick, rough, and smelled of fish oil. She tied it around her waist. Then she handed the other end to Odd.

"Trust the rope," she said. "Trust me. Don't trust the ground."

Odd took the rope. His grip was loose at first, then tight. He took a breath that rattled in his chest.
pages.image: A girl lying flat on a narrow cliff ledge, extending a measuring chain, while a boy with red hair stands behind her, gripping a thick knotted rope tightly; the vast drop and sea below visible in the background; tense, focused mood.

pages.text:
They went out together, one foot at a time, with Odd close behind Tam, his hand gripping the rope and his eyes wide as saucers.

"Drop is forty feet," Odd called out, his voice thin and high. "Stack is... ten yards. Maybe twelve."

Tam marked the distance on her paper. Her hand shook, but the line remained steady, like a pencil held by a very stiff teacher.

"Count the waves," Tam said. "Don't look down. Count the waves."

Odd started counting. One. Two. Three. The rhythm of the sea became a drumbeat in his ears. One. Two. Three. He stopped staring at the drop and began watching the rocks.

A small, shaky laugh escaped him, sounding like a kettle beginning to boil.

"I'm on a cliff," he said, breathless. "I'm on a cliff and I'm fine."

At the end of the ledge stood the old lighthouse. It was stubby and half-fallen, with a broken stair spiraling up into the dark. Tam climbed it, and Odd followed, his face tight with fear but his feet sure.

From the top, the world opened up. The entire coast stretched out before them, a long, sweeping curve of white and grey and green. It was all there. All of it.

Tam uncapped her ink. She didn't draw a line. She drew the shape. It was the best thing she had ever drawn.
pages.image: A girl climbing a broken stone spiral staircase inside a ruined lighthouse tower, with a boy following closely; outside the broken walls, a vast panoramic view of a rugged coastline and the sea under a bright sky; awe, wonder.

pages.text:
They descended the broken spiral stairs first, then faced the ledge, where Odd moved with the caution of a cat crossing a busy market street. He fixed his eyes on the grass below, ignoring the dizzying drop, and when his boots finally thumped onto solid ground, he did not run. He simply sat down.

He buried his face in his hands, then looked up at Tam, his cheeks streaked with salt spray and something else.

"Nobody in my family has touched a cliff in a hundred years," he said, his voice cracking like a dry twig. "My father insists the sea is a place you stay away from."

Tam sat beside him and unrolled her paper. The line she had drawn from the top was there, long and true and strong.

"Then we will prove him wrong," Tam said.

She pulled a tiny piece of red chalk from her satchel. At the edge of the map, near the lighthouse, she drew a small figure with red hair and arms outstretched, waving to no one in particular.

Odd stared at the red mark, then at Tam. A smile spread across his face, wide and gap-toothed, the kind of grin that appears only after a terrible ordeal has ended. It was the smile of a boy who had just conquered a monster.
pages.image: Two children sitting on green grass at the base of a high cliff, looking at a map; the boy has red hair and a wide, relieved smile, the girl has a black braid and ink-stained hands; the white cliff face rises behind them; warm, triumphant mood.

pages.text:
The sun climbed high, and the wind settled into a low, contented hum, while Tam and Odd packed their kit with the smooth, practiced rhythm of two hands rowing the same boat. Tam counted on her fingers, flexing them once, twice, three times. Three days left. If the world behaved itself, they were two days' walk from Verrin. That left one day for the river crossing. A tight margin. A risky margin.

Odd turned his head east, where the sky was not blue but a heavy, bruised line of purple cloud, low and angry, looking exactly like the back of a father's hand after he has finished scolding the dog. He frowned. His eyes dropped to the dry dirt beneath their boots, then back up to the swelling dark above.

"The Aln," he said.

He did not have to finish the sentence. They both knew what rain did to the river, how the water rose to swallow the stones, and how a swollen river turned a sturdy bridge into a slithering, dangerous thing. The cloud line crept closer, silent and slow, pressing down on the cliff edge like a thumb on a bruise.
pages.image: Two children standing on a grassy field, looking up at a dark, ominous band of purple clouds gathering in the distance; the sky is split between blue and storm-grey; tense, anticipatory mood.
